item.title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, October 2026. A companion to Fast AI. All figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py. Where a figure or a sentence uses numbers from someone else’s work, the source is cited next to it and listed in the references. Where numbers are my own illustrative assumptions, the caption says so.

In short. I believe the future of AI is, to a large extent, local. But when people talk about local AI, they usually picture one big model made small enough to fit on a laptop. I see it differently: many specialised models, a memory they share, a thin harness around them, and a careful loop that lets them keep learning from the work they do. I have four reasons. The architectures of today’s largest models already moved in this direction. Simple arithmetic about memory and bandwidth favours it on a local machine. A thin harness can help small models where it no longer helps large ones. And our own brain most likely works this way: a huge set of specialised parts, a fast memory, a slow learner, and plasticity everywhere.

TipKey takeaways
  • The largest models already split themselves into experts. DeepSeek-V3 uses about 5.5% of its parameters for each word (DeepSeek-AI 2024). An ecosystem takes the same idea further, with parts you can load, swap, test and update one by one.
  • On a laptop, generating text is limited by memory bandwidth, not computation. Speed is at most bandwidth divided by the bytes read per word, so small active models win.
  • In a simple capacity model, a general model needs roughly times more domain capacity than a specialist, where is the share of its training devoted to that domain.
  • Recent work suggests elaborate harnesses add little around strong frontier models (Brilliantov et al. 2026). For small local models, I argue the opposite: verifiers, tools and structure are where they gain the most.
  • Our brain seems to combine specialised areas, a domain-general coordinating network, a fast memory, a slow learner that consolidates during sleep, and plasticity (Fedorenko et al. 2024; Duncan et al. 2020; McClelland et al. 1995; Dehaene and Cohen 2007).
  • Memory belongs outside the weights, where people can read, correct and delete it. Learning belongs in a slow, tested loop.

1. The wrong picture

Models are getting smaller for the same capability. Xiao and colleagues measured this as capability density, and found that for open models it doubled roughly every three to three and a half months between 2023 and 2025 (Xiao et al. 2024). Better training, better architectures, quantisation and better chips all push in the same direction. I am convinced a large part of AI will move closer to where the work happens: onto our laptops, phones, machines and private servers.

But the picture most of us have in mind is one giant brain, waiting to be compressed into a smaller box. The question becomes “how much of the big model can I run locally?”, and the answer is always “a bit less than you would like, but wait a year.”

I would rather ask a different question: what would intelligence look like if it were designed for the machine in front of me from the start?

2. What I mean by an ecosystem

By an ecosystem, I mean five parts working together on one machine:

  1. Specialists. Small models, or adapters on a shared base model, each good at one job: reading invoices, writing queries, transcribing speech, a company’s own domain.
  2. A router. A small model that decides which specialist handles a task, and when to escalate.
  3. A shared memory. Knowledge and episodes stored outside the weights, readable and correctable by people.
  4. A thin harness. The tools, checks and permissions around the models: run the tests, validate the output, keep the data local.
  5. A consolidation loop. A slow process, for example at night, that turns verified experience into small, tested updates of the specialists.

A frontier model can stay outside, as a teacher and an occasional consultant.

Part I · Why I think so

3. Today’s largest models already point this way

From dense to mixtures of experts. A classic language model is dense: to produce each word, it uses every one of its parameters. Many of today’s largest models are mixtures of experts instead. The idea goes back to Shazeer and colleagues (Shazeer et al. 2017) and was scaled up in the Switch Transformer (Fedus et al. 2022). Inside, the model is split into many sub-networks, and for each word a small gate chooses a few of them.

Two published examples make the point:

  • Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7 billion parameters, but each word uses about 12.9 billion: two of its eight experts per layer (Jiang et al. 2024).
  • DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters, but each word uses about 37 billion (DeepSeek-AI 2024). Its design is telling: in each expert layer, one shared expert is used for every word, and 8 of 256 routed experts are chosen for that word. A common core, plus specialists picked on demand.

The people who build the largest models have concluded that not everything should work on everything. But a mixture of experts is still one model. All its experts must be loaded in memory, even if only a few work at a time. They are trained together, so you cannot replace one without touching the others. And they are not specialists a person would recognise: an expert is a part of the network that training happened to route certain words to.

The other pieces already exist too. What I call an ecosystem is mostly an assembly of things that already work:

  • Shared base plus adapters, in production. Apple’s on-device model has about 3 billion parameters and uses small, task-specific LoRA adapters that are swapped in for each task; a rank-16 adapter takes tens of megabytes (Gunter et al. 2024; Hu et al. 2022).
  • Many adapters on one machine. S-LoRA showed how to serve thousands of adapters on top of one base model (Sheng et al. 2023).
  • Experts trained separately. Branch-Train-MiX trains domain experts in parallel from a common starting model, then combines them (Sukhbaatar et al. 2024).
  • Routing between models. RouteLLM learns when a query can go to a cheaper model, and reports cost reductions of more than two times on some benchmarks without a loss in quality (Ong et al. 2025). FrugalGPT reports matching the best single model with large cost savings by cascading models (Chen et al. 2023).
  • Memory outside the weights. RETRO, with retrieval from a large text database, performs comparably to GPT-3 on the Pile benchmark with about 25 times fewer parameters (Borgeaud et al. 2022; Lewis et al. 2020).

None of these is the whole ecosystem. Together, they show that each part is not speculation. Researchers at NVIDIA recently made a similar case for agents: most of what agents do is a small number of repetitive, specialised tasks, which small models can handle more economically, with larger models called only when needed (Belcak et al. 2025).

4. The arithmetic of a laptop: bandwidth

This is the argument I find most convincing, because it is simple arithmetic.

When a model generates text for one person, each new word requires reading all the active weights from memory once, and doing roughly two operations per weight. With weights stored at bits, a model with active parameters reads bytes per word. The speed is therefore bounded by the memory bandwidth :

Is bandwidth really the limit, and not computation? The roofline model answers this by comparing operations per byte (Williams et al. 2009). Decoding for one user at 4 bits does about two operations per half byte, so about 4 operations per byte read. A laptop GPU that can do tens of trillions of operations per second, with a bandwidth of about 500 GB/s, needs tens of operations per byte to be kept busy. Decoding offers far fewer, so it waits for memory.

Take a laptop with 128 GB of memory and up to 546 GB/s of bandwidth, the published figures for Apple’s M4 Max (Apple 2024). I use 500 GB/s and 4-bit weights:

Model Active parameters Read per word Upper bound
3B specialist 3B 1.5 GB ≈ 330 words/s
8B specialist 8B 4 GB ≈ 125 words/s
70B dense model 70B 35 GB ≈ 14 words/s
DeepSeek-V3 (MoE) 37B of 671B 18.5 GB ≈ 27 words/s, but 335 GB does not fit in 128 GB

Two consequences follow. The same 128 GB that cannot hold one frontier model can hold about thirty 8-billion-parameter specialists, each of them fast. And this wall is not going away soon: over two decades, peak compute of server hardware grew about 3.0 times every two years, but memory bandwidth only about 1.6 times (Gholami et al. 2024). Techniques such as speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023) help, but they help small models just as much as large ones.

5. The arithmetic of capacity: why specialists can be small

The second argument is about where a model spends its capacity.

Michaud and colleagues proposed a useful way to think about scaling: knowledge comes in discrete units, which they call quanta, used with very different frequencies, and a model learns them roughly in order of how often they are needed (Michaud et al. 2023). Here is a simple consequence, in my own words and with my own simplifications.

Suppose a task needs two kinds of quanta: a shared core (language, basic reasoning), which takes parameters, and domain knowledge, which takes . A specialist needs both:

A general model is trained on everything, and the domain is only a share of what it sees. In the simplest symmetric case, where many domains each have a share and similar structure, the general model reaches the same depth in this domain only when it has learned as deep into every other domain too:

With illustrative values of 2 billion for the core and 1 billion for the domain, a domain that is 1% of the general model’s training needs about 102 billion parameters for the same depth, against 3 billion for the specialist.

The model is crude, and its main assumption, that domains do not help each other beyond the shared core, is not fully true. Knowledge does transfer between domains, and a general model like GPT-4, carefully prompted, has outperformed specialist medical models on medical benchmarks (Nori et al. 2023). That is exactly why the formula keeps : a good specialist is not trained from scratch, it starts from a strong shared core.

The published evidence is consistent with the direction of the argument. A 770-million-parameter model trained with explanations from a much larger model outperformed few-shot prompted 540-billion-parameter PaLM on a benchmark, using only 80% of the training data (Hsieh et al. 2023). A 1.3-billion-parameter model trained on carefully chosen data reached 50.6% on the HumanEval coding benchmark (Gunasekar et al. 2023). Narrow, well-taught models can be very small.

6. The arithmetic of many specialists: adapters

If every specialist were a separate model, memory would fill up quickly. Adapters solve much of this.

A LoRA adapter replaces the update of a weight matrix of size by two thin matrices of rank (Hu et al. 2022). Its size relative to the matrix is

With and , that is about 1%. Applied to a 3-billion-parameter base model, an adapter has roughly 30 million parameters, about 60 MB at 16 bits, consistent with the “tens of megabytes” Apple reports for its rank-16 adapters (Gunter et al. 2024).

One hundred specialists as adapters take about 7.5 GB; as separate models, 150 GB. There is a trade-off, and it is worth knowing: adapters learn less than full fine-tuning, but they also forget less of what the base model knew (Biderman et al. 2024). For a system that must keep learning without breaking, forgetting less is a feature.

7. The arithmetic of routing

An ecosystem is only as good as its router. A simple model makes this precise.

Let be the router’s accuracy, the quality when a task reaches the right specialist, and the quality when it reaches the wrong one. The expected quality is

The ecosystem beats one general model of quality that runs at a similar speed only if

With illustrative values , and , the router must be right more than 83% of the time. If the router also knows when it is unsure, and sends half of its mistakes to a larger model with quality , the threshold drops to about 64%.

The lesson is not the exact numbers, which are mine. It is the shape: a router that knows its own uncertainty is worth more than a slightly better specialist. This is also what makes published routing work encouraging (Ong et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2023).

8. The harness: thin around strong models, essential around small ones

A recent study from EPFL and Apple asks how much of a harness (the orchestrators, sub-agents and retrieval layers built around a model) a strong agent needs for machine-learning engineering tasks. Under an equal time budget and the same frontier model, the elaborate open-source harnesses they tested gave no advantage over a single session of a minimal coding agent with direct access to read, write and run commands (Brilliantov et al. 2026). Their conclusion is that the model is the main driver of performance, and that elaborate harnesses around strong models give poor returns on current benchmarks.

At first sight, this goes against an ecosystem. If structure around a model does not help, why build an ecosystem at all? I read it differently, for three reasons.

First, it is a result about strong models. The study holds the frontier model fixed. It says that a strong model has absorbed much of what the scaffolding was doing. That fits Sutton’s “bitter lesson”: general methods that use more computation tend to beat hand-built structure in the long run (Sutton 2019). It says much less about a 3-billion-parameter model on a laptop.

Second, small models gain the most from the right kind of harness. Several results point that way:

  • The design of the interface matters: SWE-agent showed that giving a model well-designed commands to view, edit and test code improved results on software tasks, without changing the model (Yang et al. 2024).
  • A verifier turns attempts into results: with repeated attempts checked by the project’s own tests, an open model went from solving 15.9% of SWE-bench Lite issues in one attempt to 56% in 250 attempts, above the best single attempt reported at the time, 43% (Brown et al. 2024).
  • Extra computation at the time of answering, used well, allowed a smaller model to outperform a 14 times larger one, on problems where the smaller model already had a reasonable success rate (Snell et al. 2025).
  • Apple’s framework for its on-device model offers guided generation and constrained tool calling, which keep a small model’s output within a valid structure (Apple 2025).

The arithmetic is worth a sentence. If a single attempt succeeds with probability and attempts were independent, attempts would succeed with probability . In practice attempts are correlated, so the real gain is smaller, as the figure shows. But on a local machine, where a small specialist is fast and a test can check each answer, a few extra attempts cost very little.

Third, some of the harness can never be absorbed into a model. A persistent memory that lasts beyond one conversation. Permissions over what may leave the machine. Tests that decide whether an output or an update is accepted. The local data itself. However strong models become, these stay outside.

So my conclusion is a design rule: keep the harness thin, and keep only what earns its place. Scaffolding that compensates for weak reasoning should be removable, and removed as specialists get better. Structure that gives memory, verification and control should stay.

9. Our own brain

The last reason is closer to home. When I look at how our brain seems to be organised, it does not look like one dense model. It looks much more like an ecosystem. I want to be careful here, because biology does not prove anything about software, and the brain is not a set of neat boxes.

Many specialised parts. Neuroscience has found areas that respond to specific things. A classic example is an area of the visual cortex that responds much more strongly to faces than to other objects (Kanwisher et al. 1997). Damage to such areas can remove one ability and leave others almost intact. At the same time, representations are also distributed and overlapping across areas (Haxby et al. 2001). Specialised, but heavily connected.

Language and thinking are handled by different networks. One of the most striking recent results for my argument comes from the study of language. Brain imaging reliably finds a network that is engaged when we read or listen to sentences, and it is largely not engaged when we solve problems or reason; people who lose language through brain damage can still reason (Fedorenko et al. 2024). Mahowald and colleagues drew the consequence for AI: large language models are very good at the form of language, but their ability to reason and use it in the world is uneven, and models that work like humans may need separate mechanisms for the two (Mahowald et al. 2024).

And a general-purpose network, too. The brain is not only specialists. A multiple-demand network, spread over frontal and parietal areas, is engaged by many different demanding tasks and seems to help assemble the right parts for the problem at hand (Duncan et al. 2020). In the ecosystem, that is the role of the shared core and the router: one general part that coordinates many specialised ones.

Specialisation may simply be efficient. A recent experiment makes this more than an analogy. Dobs and colleagues trained artificial neural networks to recognise both faces and objects. Without being told to, the networks split themselves into separate systems for faces and for objects, much as the brain does (Dobs et al. 2022). Their interpretation is that specialisation is what good optimisation tends to produce when tasks are different enough.

Probably a very large number of units. Mountcastle proposed that the cortex is built from a repeated basic unit, the cortical column (Mountcastle 1997). Hawkins goes further and suggests that each column builds its own model of the world, and that they reach decisions together (Hawkins 2021); his team has since started an open project that builds AI from many such repeated learning modules (Clay et al. 2024). This is a theory, and it is debated. But the picture of a large number of similar units, each specialised by what it receives, is widely shared.

A fast memory and a slow learner. The theory of complementary learning systems proposes that the hippocampus learns new episodes quickly, while the neocortex learns slowly, by replaying those episodes over time (McClelland et al. 1995; Kumaran et al. 2016). Replay during sleep was first observed in the hippocampus of rats (Wilson and McNaughton 1994), and it has since been measured in humans as well, during rest (Liu et al. 2019; Schuck and Niv 2019). Sleep seems to play an active role in moving memories from the fast system to the slow one (Klinzing et al. 2019). One reason for two systems is precisely to avoid what AI researchers call catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989).

Plasticity. Connections change with use. And when we learn to read, a region of the visual cortex becomes specialised for written words, a process Dehaene and Cohen call neuronal recycling (Dehaene and Cohen 2007). New specialists are not only present from birth; they are formed during life.

Sparse and frugal. The human brain has about 86 billion neurons (Herculano-Houzel 2009) and runs on roughly 20 watts (Balasubramanian 2021). Energy budgets suggest that only a small share of cortical neurons can be strongly active at the same time, perhaps around one percent, although the exact figure is debated (Lennie 2003; Attwell and Laughlin 2001).

Researchers who work on lifelong learning in machines draw the same lesson from biology: memory systems that learn at different speeds, replay, and modular, adaptable parts are among the mechanisms they consider most promising (Kudithipudi et al. 2022). If our best example of general intelligence is most likely a huge set of specialised, plastic sub-models, with a general coordinator, a fast memory and a slow learner, then I find it hard to believe that the best local AI will be one frozen, dense block.

Part II · The ecosystem in practice

10. A memory outside the weights

Specialists need a memory they share. In Fast AI I argued that a large model should be used to build a structured memory, such as a knowledge graph experts can inspect and correct. In a local ecosystem, that memory becomes the common ground, and plays the role of the fast memory in section 9. Two kinds matter:

  • Knowledge: facts, rules, relations. “This customer always pays within 30 days.”
  • Episodes: what happened. “Last Tuesday this invoice was rejected because the supplier’s VAT number did not match.”

Keeping this memory outside the weights is what makes the system trustworthy. You can read it. You can correct a fact in one place, and every specialist benefits. You can delete something and know it is gone, which is very hard to guarantee once data has been used to train a model; removing its influence afterwards is an open research problem (Bourtoule et al. 2021). Retrieval also lets small models know far more than their weights hold (Borgeaud et al. 2022; Lewis et al. 2020).

This is, for me, the strongest reason for running it locally. Privacy is not only protection. It is the condition for memory. People and companies will only let a system remember everything useful if they control where that memory lives.

11. A way to keep learning

A memory lets a system look things up. It does not let it get better. Today’s models are trained once, frozen, and shipped. A local ecosystem can do better, because it sees the same kind of work every day, and because its specialists are small enough to update. I imagine a loop with two speeds, inspired by section 9:

  1. Fast, during the day. The specialists work. Successes, corrections and failures are written to the memory as episodes. Nothing in the models changes.
  2. Slow, at night. The system selects verified episodes, mixes them with examples of what the specialist already does well, updates the adapter, and tests the result against everything it was already good at. If it is better and has not forgotten anything, it is kept. If not, it is rolled back.

Each step has support in existing work. Mixing old examples with new ones, replay, is one of the most reliable ways to limit forgetting (Rolnick et al. 2019); brain-inspired versions of replay go further and replay internal representations instead of stored examples (Ven et al. 2020). Other methods protect the weights that matter most for old tasks (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017). Adapters forget less than full fine-tuning (Biderman et al. 2024). And using a machine’s idle time is starting to be studied as a resource in itself: sleep-time compute lets a model think about its context before questions arrive, reducing the work needed when they do (Lin et al. 2025). A broad review of continual learning describes the trade-offs between these approaches (Wang et al. 2024).

The test step deserves a little arithmetic, because it is where narrow specialists have a real advantage. If a specialist is right with probability on a test set of examples, the standard error of the measured accuracy is

With and , percentage points, so a drop of 2 points stands out at about three standard errors. Building 2000 good test cases for one narrow job is realistic. Building them for every ability of a general model is not.

The risks are real. A model trained repeatedly on its own outputs can degrade, a problem known as model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024). The risk is much lower when real data are kept and accumulated alongside generated data, instead of being replaced by it (Gerstgrasser et al. 2024). This is one more reason for a memory that keeps the real episodes, and for a loop that learns only from episodes verified by a test, a person or the real world, never from its own unchecked answers. And a model that changes every night is harder to certify. Small updates, strict tests, a memory that keeps the evidence, and the ability to roll back are not optional.

12. Where the big models fit

None of this makes frontier models useless. It changes their role.

They become teachers: their knowledge can be passed to small models by distillation (Hinton et al. 2015), including their step-by-step explanations (Hsieh et al. 2023). The DeepSeek-R1 team, for example, released a family of small models, from 1.5 to 70 billion parameters, trained on the reasoning of its large model (DeepSeek-AI 2025). They become architects of memory: they read the documents and build the first version of the knowledge graph. And they become consultants: when the router meets something new, or a problem that needs broad reasoning across many domains, it can ask, with the user’s permission, and the verified answer becomes an episode the local system can learn from.

13. What would prove me wrong

An essay that argues for a future should say what would change the author’s mind. Mine would change if:

  • general small models kept beating ecosystems of specialists using the same memory, even with good routing;
  • routers could not reach the accuracy that the arithmetic in section 7 requires on real, messy work;
  • nightly updates could not pass strict regression tests without forgetting, even with replay and adapters;
  • memory bandwidth on consumer devices grew fast enough that a single large model ran comfortably everywhere.

I do not think these will happen, but they are measurable, and I intend to keep watching.

14. Conclusion

I do not think we should wait for the big brain to come to us. The future I believe in is already within reach, and it is organised differently: specialists that are excellent at one thing, a router that knows who does what and when it does not know, a memory you own, a harness that is thin but keeps the essentials, and a careful loop that turns yesterday’s verified work into tomorrow’s skill.

The question will not only be “how much intelligence can I run locally?” It will be “how well is my local intelligence organised, what does it remember, and how does it learn?” Our own brain, most likely, already answers it that way.

item.title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, October 2026. A follow-up to A Universe Without a Bottom. Everything is open: download the code and results (zip, 2 MB), browse them on GitHub, or read the working paper (PDF, 4 pages).

In short. A physics paper about how structure appears out of complete disorder made me ask a question I could actually test: while an AI image generator turns noise into a picture, where does the picture’s information live, in the inside of a region or on its border? I ran the experiment in one evening, on two CPU cores, with an AI as lab partner. Finished images follow an area law: information lives on borders. But on the way, the big decisions are made across the whole image first, and only later settle onto the edges. I also found a way to measure this inside any image generator using nothing but its ability to remove noise, and checked it against exact answers. None of this is my field. The part I want to stress is how it was possible at all.

TipKey takeaways
  • Finished handwritten digits follow an area law (β = 1.07): what a patch shares with the rest of the image grows with its border.
  • In the noisy early phase, real structure adds up to 2.4 times more shared information than a control, and it grows more like the patch’s size. Structure is decided in the bulk and written on the boundary.
  • The change is smooth. A “sudden transition” seen in one early run was noise, and disappeared when repeated.
  • The same information can be read from denoising errors alone (median difference 3% from the exact values), so the method can be applied to real, trained image generators.
  • An AI lab partner did not give me the answers. It let me ask the question properly: build, run, check, criticise, and throw away what does not hold.

Part I · From the cosmos to code

1. It must be simpler than this

Recently I wrote about reading a physics paper I could not follow: Holograms and Standard Models, by Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind. My first reaction was simple. Something is wrong here. It must be easier. I believe the universe is fundamentally simple.

That essay ended in philosophy. Grains inside grains, nothing creating everything, and the idea that the meaning is in the middle.

This one ends in an experiment.

I am a software architect, not a physicist. But I kept coming back to one idea from that paper, and one evening I asked a different question: could I actually test something? Not about the universe. About the AI systems I work with every day.

2. The surface knows everything

The idea that stuck is the holographic principle. In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking found that the information a black hole can hold depends on the area of its surface, not on its volume. Double its size and its information grows four times, not eight.

Physicists found the same pattern elsewhere. In many systems, the information shared between a region and everything around it grows with the region’s boundary. They call it an area law. When it grows with the region’s size instead, it is a volume law.

Susskind and his colleagues go further. They build a small world of particles and forces from a system at infinite temperature, the state of maximum disorder, the closest thing to “nothing” physics allows. Structure from nothing, organised on a surface.

I could not check their mathematics. But their question felt general: when structure appears out of complete disorder, where does its information live?

3. A machine that builds structure from disorder

Then I realised I already knew a machine that builds structure from disorder.

Image generators like Stable Diffusion are diffusion models. They start from pure random noise, the same maximum-disorder state, and remove the noise step by step until an image appears. A face, a cat, a handwritten digit.

The universe gives us one run, seen from inside, mostly through a horizon. A diffusion model gives us as many runs as we want, and we can stop it at any moment and look.

So the question became concrete. While an image forms out of noise, does the information shared between a patch of the image and the rest of it grow with the patch’s border, or with its size? Area or volume? And does that change along the way?

Part II · The experiment

4. What I measured

The measurement is simple to state. Take a square patch of an image. Ask how much knowing the rest of the image tells you about that patch. Physicists call this mutual information. Then make the patch bigger and watch how that number grows.

If it grows like the border of the patch, it is an area law. If it grows like the number of pixels inside, it is a volume law. I summarise the growth with one number, β, from

where is the side of the patch in pixels: β close to 1 means area law, close to 2 means volume law.

I did not use a giant neural network. I used something I could compute exactly: a statistical model of handwritten digits (the classic MNIST dataset) built from 40 simple pieces, four per digit. It learns real structure; on images it has never seen, it is far better than a simple model. And for this kind of model, every stage between noise and finished image can be calculated precisely, with no training noise and no guessing.

The most important part is the comparison. For every measurement I also built a control: a much simpler model that has exactly the same correlations between pixels but none of the real structure. No strokes, no digits, just smooth statistical blur. Whatever the real model does that the control does not, comes from actual structure. Without that control, I would have fooled myself at least twice.

5. What I found

Finished digits follow an area law. At the end of generation, β is 1.07. The information a patch shares with the rest of the image grows with its border.

But on the way, something else happens. In the noisy early phase, the real model carries up to 2.4 times more shared information than the control, and that extra information grows more like the size of the patch than its border. As the image sharpens, the extra information moves toward the borders, and the two curves meet (Figure 1).

Here is how I read it. Early on, the model is deciding the big things: which digit, roughly where, which way it leans. That is a fact about the whole image, and every pixel carries a little evidence about it, so it scales with size. Later, the model draws the details: strokes, edges, where black meets white. Those are local, and they live on borders.

Or, in one line: structure is decided in the bulk and written on the boundary.

6. What did not work

I expected a sudden switch, like water turning to ice, at one precise moment. A first coarse run seemed to show one. When I repeated it with eleven noise levels and three independent runs, the jump disappeared. The change is smooth (Figure 2). The “sudden switch” was noise in a single run.

I keep it in the story because it is exactly the kind of mistake that is easy to publish and hard to take back.

7. What it does not show

I asked for a tough review of my own results, the kind a referee would write. Here is what holds up less well than I would like.

  • The area law alone is not surprising. Any image whose pixels mostly correlate with their neighbours gives an area law. Physicists have known this for years. The new part is not the final area law but the extra structure and how it moves from bulk to boundary.
  • It describes the data, not the network. Because I computed everything exactly, the results describe what noisy digits look like at each stage, which is the same for any perfect generator. To say how real neural networks behave, I need to test a trained one.
  • The images are tiny. At 28×28 pixels I can only compare patches from 2 to 12 pixels wide. That is less than one order of magnitude, and the blank border of each digit distorts larger patches.
  • The physics is an analogy. A black hole’s surface and the border of an image patch are not the same thing. The parallel is suggestive, and testable, but it is not a proof of anything about the universe.

None of this makes the work worthless. It tells me exactly what to do next.

Part III · Pushing past the limit

8. Seeing inside any generator

The second limitation bothered me most. My exact method only works on simple models. Real generators, the ones people actually use, are giant neural networks where nothing can be computed exactly.

Then I came across a result from information theory, from 2005, by Guo, Shamai and Verdú. It links information to how hard it is to remove noise. Applied to my question, it says something I find beautiful:

The information a patch shares with the rest of the image equals how much seeing the rest helps you clean up that patch, added up over all noise levels.

In symbols, with the patch, the rest of the image and the error of the best possible denoiser at a given signal-to-noise ratio :

That matters because cleaning up noise is exactly what a diffusion model is trained to do. So in principle you could measure the information map of any generator just by asking it to denoise a patch twice: once seeing only the patch, once seeing the whole image.

I tested this on my digit model, where I already knew the exact answer. The two routes agree, with a median difference of 3% across 32 comparisons (patch sizes from 2 to 12 pixels, noise levels from heavy to light). The largest difference was 14%, on one very small, very noisy patch (Figure 3).

This is the part I find most valuable. The exact calculations become a ground truth to check a method that can scale to real models. The next step is to run it on a trained neural network. That needs a model that can denoise with part of the image hidden, which many image generators already can.

9. You don’t need a big machine

Everything in this essay ran on two CPU cores. No GPU, no cloud cluster, no downloaded giant model. The longest run took about seven minutes.

At one point I was told the next step needed a GPU. I pushed back: why should a question need a big machine? It turned out the honest answer was that only one specific claim needs it, the one about trained neural networks. Everything else, the exact calculations, the controls, the repeated runs, fits on a laptop. Some of the best physics ever done was tabletop physics. A well-controlled small experiment beats a sloppy big one.

Part IV · What the AI made possible

10. A lab partner, not an oracle

I should be transparent about how this was done. I did it in one evening with Claude, Anthropic’s AI, as a lab partner. I brought the questions and the stubbornness; it wrote and ran the code, searched the literature, and, importantly, reviewed the results harshly when I asked it to. It also caught its own mistakes: a model that looked better than it was, a chart label that overstated a result, a “sudden transition” that was not there.

Look back at the path of this essay and count the steps that would have stopped me alone:

  • From a feeling to a measurable question. “It must be simpler” is not a hypothesis. Turning it into “does mutual information scale with the border or the size, and does that change along the generation path?” took a conversation, not a degree.
  • From a question to code that runs. Exact mutual information for a 784-pixel mixture model, Monte Carlo estimates with error bars, a fair control. Each is a week of reading for an outsider. Here, each was a script I could read, run and question within minutes.
  • From a result to a result I trust. The control model, the three independent runs, the fine grid of noise levels: these exist because I kept asking “how would I fool myself here?”, and the answers came back as experiments, not opinions.
  • From a dead end to a way forward. The method that works on real generators comes from a 2005 information-theory paper I had never heard of. Finding it, understanding what it says about my question, and testing it against the exact values all happened in the same evening.
  • From a claim to a smaller, honest claim. The harsh review took the area law off its pedestal and left the more interesting part standing. The GPU question turned “this needs a big machine” into “only this one claim does”.

None of these steps is new science on its own. What is new, for me, is that they can follow each other at the speed of curiosity. The distance between “I wonder whether…” and “here is the plot, here is the control, here is why it might be wrong” used to be months, and for someone outside the field it was usually infinite. That evening it was hours.

11. Innovation is in the asking

This is the part of AI I find most interesting. Not that it answers, but that it lets someone like me ask properly: run the experiment, check it, and throw away what does not hold.

It is tempting to say that AI will produce new ideas by itself. I do not think that is what happened here. The question came from me, reading a paper I could not follow and refusing to let it go. The direction changed three times because of judgement calls: insist on a control, distrust a jump that looked too good, refuse to accept that a question needs a big machine. What the AI removed was the cost of each step in between. When trying an idea costs minutes instead of weeks, you try more of them, you kill the bad ones sooner, and the good ones get pushed further than you would ever have pushed them alone.

That also changes what rigour means for an outsider. The danger of a fast partner is that you go fast in the wrong direction, and a confident AI can make a wrong result look finished. The defence is the same as in any lab: controls, repeated runs, a referee who is paid to be unkind, and everything published so that others can check. The AI can play the referee too, if you ask it to. You have to ask.

Part V · Back to the beginning

12. A very good middle

I started with a feeling: the universe must be simpler than that paper. I still believe it. But I see now that simple does not mean easy, and it does not mean finished.

In my last essay I wrote that “from nothing to nothing” forgets the middle, and that the middle is everything. This experiment is a small version of that idea. A machine starts from noise, from nothing. It ends with a digit, a finished thing. And in between, there is a moment where the big decisions are made everywhere at once, before they settle quietly onto the edges.

I don’t know if the universe works like that. I do know that a question asked on a quiet evening can become something you can measure. That is not the end of anything. It is a very good middle.

13. Try it yourself

Everything is open. You can rerun every number and every figure in this essay on an ordinary laptop in about half an hour.

  • Code and results: download as a zip, or browse on GitHub. It contains all scripts, the result files, the figures, and a run_all.sh that reproduces everything. The only thing to download is the MNIST dataset (about 11 MB); the README gives the link. MIT licence.
  • Working paper: From Noise to Boundaries: Area-Law Information Scaling Along the Diffusion Path, a four-page technical version with the equations and references.
  • Requirements: Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib. No GPU.
Step Script What it does Time (2 CPU cores)

If you work on diffusion models, information theory or the physics of learning, I would love your critique, especially on the denoising-error method and how to test it on a trained network. And if you are, like me, someone outside the field with a question that will not leave you alone: try it. You may not need a bigger machine. You may just need a smaller experiment, and a good partner to run it with.

item.title: A Universe Without a Bottom
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Something different, just this once. This blog is usually about AI, machines and measurement. This essay is not. It is a personal detour into physics, written by someone who is neither a physicist nor a mathematician, following a question out of curiosity. Its follow-up, Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary, brings the question back to AI.

It must be simpler than this

I am not a physicist. I am not a mathematician. But one evening I opened a new physics paper, Holograms and Standard Models by Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind, and tried to follow it.

I got lost quickly. Fermions, ensembles, double-scaled limits, Feynman diagrams that look like flowers. And my first reaction was simple: something is wrong here. It must be easier. I believe the universe is fundamentally simple.

This essay is what happened when I followed that feeling. I didn’t find the answer. I found better questions, and maybe that is the point.

The surface knows everything

The first surprise came from black holes. In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking found that the information a black hole can hold depends on the area of its surface, not on its volume.

In plain words: cover the horizon with tiny tiles, each the size of the smallest length physics knows, and you have counted everything inside. Double the size of the black hole and its information grows four times, not eight.

This is strange. In everyday life a bigger box holds more things because it has more room inside. Here the inside seems to be written on the walls. Physicists call this the holographic principle: our three-dimensional world may be like an image projected from a flat surface.

So I asked myself: what if area and volume are not two different things? What if they are two faces of the same idea? It turns out physicists ask this too. Some say the area measures how much things are connected (entanglement) and the volume measures how complicated they are. Maybe space is just the shape that information takes when we look at it from inside.

Everything from nothing

Einstein did not change physics with more complicated equations. He took one simple idea completely seriously: light moves at the same speed for everyone. So I wondered if we are looking in the wrong place. What if there is nothing at all, and that nothing is creating everything?

To my surprise, the paper I could not follow says something close to this. The authors put their model at infinite temperature. That sounds extreme, but it means something simple: every possibility is equally likely. No preference, no structure, no information. It is the state of maximum ignorance, the closest thing to “nothing” that quantum physics allows.

And from this featureless state they claim a whole small world appears: particles, forces, even the tiny energy of empty space. Their motto is “set it and forget it.” You choose one number, how big the system is, and the rest follows.

Others had similar dreams. Some physicists noticed that the energy of matter and the energy of gravity may cancel exactly, so a universe might cost nothing to make. John Wheeler said “it from bit”: reality built from yes-or-no answers, information before matter. Of course, their “nothing” still has laws of physics in it. Why there are laws at all is still a mystery.

Grains within grains

Then another thought. What if we never reach the final piece? What if there is no end?

History points that way. We thought atoms were the bottom. Then we found the nucleus, then quarks. Each time the “fundamental” level turned out to be made of something else.

But the black hole formula seems to say no. If a region can hold only a limited amount of information, it cannot hide infinite layers inside. There must be a floor.

Unless the floor belongs only to us. What if what we call the universe is just one grain? The limit would apply inside our horizon, the part we can see, and not to everything. Some cosmologists already imagine this: space inflating forever, making bubble universes like ours, each one a grain, each with its own rules.

And it should work both ways. In 1987 physicists showed that a tiny bubble of very dense energy could grow into a new universe. From outside it would look like a small black hole that disappears. From inside it would be a whole cosmos, expanding, maybe one day full of people asking the same questions. A grain inside our grain. And maybe ours is a grain inside someone else’s.

The vertigo

At this point I felt something I did not expect. A kind of dizziness. Nothing creating everything. Grains inside grains. No final layer. Are we at the end of thinking, or just getting close to going a bit mad?

I don’t think it is madness. Pascal, more than three hundred years ago, wrote that the eternal silence of infinite spaces frightened him. Einstein said the most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible. The dizziness seems to be what you feel when you follow the questions honestly.

The hard part is not the physics. It is accepting that we may go from nothing to nothing, with no final answer waiting for us. We want an end. We tell stories with endings. We look for the cause behind the cause. Being told the chain may never close feels like losing the ground under your feet.

The meaning is in the middle

Mathematics went through this once. In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that mathematics can never be complete: there will always be true things it cannot prove. Many thought it was the end. It was not. Mathematics kept growing, and the open horizon became part of its beauty.

Maybe physics is the same. An end out of reach does not make the answers along the way less real. Feynman said he could live with doubt and not knowing, and that it was more interesting than having answers that might be wrong.

And “from nothing to nothing” forgets the middle. The middle is everything: stars, black holes, and someone on a quiet evening trying to understand a paper too difficult for them. If there is no final end, then asking is not a failure to arrive. Maybe it is what the universe does when it becomes complex enough to look at itself.

I started by believing the universe must be simple. I still believe it. But maybe simple does not mean finished.

Quelque chose de différent, pour une fois. Ce blog parle d’habitude d’IA, de machines et de mesure. Pas cet essai. C’est un détour personnel par la physique, écrit par quelqu’un qui n’est ni physicien ni mathématicien, et qui suit une question par curiosité. Sa suite, Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary (en anglais), ramène la question vers l’IA. Traduit de l’anglais : version originale.

Ça doit être plus simple que ça

Je ne suis pas physicien. Je ne suis pas mathématicien. Mais un soir, j’ai ouvert un nouvel article de physique, Holograms and Standard Models de Miyashita, Sekino et Susskind, et j’ai essayé de le suivre.

Je me suis vite perdu. Des fermions, des ensembles, des limites doublement mises à l’échelle, des diagrammes de Feynman qui ressemblent à des fleurs. Et ma première réaction a été simple : quelque chose ne va pas. Ça doit être plus facile. Je crois que l’univers est fondamentalement simple.

Cet essai raconte ce qui s’est passé quand j’ai suivi ce sentiment. Je n’ai pas trouvé la réponse. J’ai trouvé de meilleures questions, et c’est peut-être cela, l’essentiel.

La surface sait tout

La première surprise est venue des trous noirs. Dans les années 1970, Bekenstein et Hawking ont découvert que l’information qu’un trou noir peut contenir dépend de l’aire de sa surface, et non de son volume.

En termes simples : couvrez l’horizon de minuscules tuiles, chacune de la taille de la plus petite longueur que connaît la physique, et vous avez compté tout ce qu’il y a à l’intérieur. Doublez la taille du trou noir, et son information est multipliée par quatre, pas par huit.

C’est étrange. Dans la vie de tous les jours, une boîte plus grande contient plus de choses parce qu’elle a plus de place à l’intérieur. Ici, l’intérieur semble écrit sur les murs. Les physiciens appellent cela le principe holographique : notre monde en trois dimensions pourrait être comme une image projetée depuis une surface plane.

Alors je me suis demandé : et si l’aire et le volume n’étaient pas deux choses différentes ? Et s’ils étaient les deux faces d’une même idée ? Il se trouve que les physiciens se le demandent aussi. Certains disent que l’aire mesure à quel point les choses sont connectées (l’intrication) et que le volume mesure à quel point elles sont compliquées. L’espace n’est peut-être que la forme que prend l’information quand on la regarde de l’intérieur.

Tout à partir de rien

Einstein n’a pas changé la physique avec des équations plus compliquées. Il a pris une idée simple complètement au sérieux : la lumière se déplace à la même vitesse pour tout le monde. Alors je me suis demandé si nous ne cherchions pas au mauvais endroit. Et s’il n’y avait rien du tout, et que ce rien créait tout ?

À ma surprise, l’article que je n’arrivais pas à suivre dit quelque chose de proche. Les auteurs placent leur modèle à température infinie. Cela semble extrême, mais cela veut dire quelque chose de simple : toutes les possibilités sont également probables. Aucune préférence, aucune structure, aucune information. C’est l’état d’ignorance maximale, ce qui ressemble le plus à « rien » dans ce que permet la physique quantique.

Et de cet état sans relief, ils affirment qu’un petit monde entier apparaît : des particules, des forces, et même la minuscule énergie de l’espace vide. Leur devise est « set it and forget it », réglez et oubliez. On choisit un seul nombre, la taille du système, et le reste suit.

D’autres ont fait des rêves semblables. Certains physiciens ont remarqué que l’énergie de la matière et celle de la gravité pourraient s’annuler exactement, si bien qu’un univers pourrait ne rien coûter à fabriquer. John Wheeler disait « it from bit » : la réalité construite à partir de réponses par oui ou par non, l’information avant la matière. Bien sûr, leur « rien » contient encore les lois de la physique. Pourquoi il y a des lois, cela reste un mystère.

Des grains dans des grains

Puis une autre pensée. Et si nous n’atteignions jamais la dernière pièce ? Et s’il n’y avait pas de fin ?

L’histoire va dans ce sens. Nous pensions que les atomes étaient le fond. Puis nous avons trouvé le noyau, puis les quarks. Chaque fois, le niveau « fondamental » s’est révélé fait d’autre chose.

Mais la formule du trou noir semble dire non. Si une région ne peut contenir qu’une quantité limitée d’information, elle ne peut pas cacher une infinité de couches à l’intérieur. Il doit y avoir un plancher.

À moins que ce plancher ne soit le nôtre seulement. Et si ce que nous appelons l’univers n’était qu’un grain ? La limite s’appliquerait à l’intérieur de notre horizon, la partie que nous pouvons voir, et pas à tout. Certains cosmologistes imaginent déjà cela : un espace qui gonfle sans fin, produisant des univers-bulles comme le nôtre, chacun un grain, chacun avec ses propres règles.

Et cela devrait marcher dans les deux sens. En 1987, des physiciens ont montré qu’une minuscule bulle d’énergie très dense pourrait devenir un nouvel univers. Vue de l’extérieur, elle ressemblerait à un petit trou noir qui disparaît. Vue de l’intérieur, ce serait un cosmos entier, en expansion, peut-être un jour peuplé de gens qui se posent les mêmes questions. Un grain à l’intérieur de notre grain. Et peut-être le nôtre est-il un grain à l’intérieur de celui de quelqu’un d’autre.

Le vertige

À ce stade, j’ai ressenti quelque chose que je n’attendais pas. Une sorte de vertige. Le rien qui crée tout. Des grains dans des grains. Pas de dernière couche. Sommes-nous au bout de la pensée, ou simplement en train de devenir un peu fous ?

Je ne crois pas que ce soit de la folie. Pascal, il y a plus de trois cents ans, écrivait : « Le silence éternel de ces espaces infinis m’effraie. » Einstein disait que ce qu’il y a de plus incompréhensible dans l’univers, c’est qu’il soit compréhensible. Le vertige semble être ce que l’on ressent quand on suit les questions honnêtement.

Le plus difficile n’est pas la physique. C’est d’accepter que nous allons peut-être de rien à rien, sans réponse finale qui nous attend. Nous voulons une fin. Nous racontons des histoires qui ont une fin. Nous cherchons la cause derrière la cause. Entendre que la chaîne ne se refermera peut-être jamais, c’est comme sentir le sol se dérober sous ses pieds.

Le sens est au milieu

Les mathématiques sont déjà passées par là. En 1931, Kurt Gödel a prouvé que les mathématiques ne pourront jamais être complètes : il y aura toujours des choses vraies qu’elles ne peuvent pas démontrer. Beaucoup ont cru que c’était la fin. Ce ne l’était pas. Les mathématiques ont continué de grandir, et l’horizon ouvert est devenu une part de leur beauté.

Peut-être la physique est-elle pareille. Une fin hors d’atteinte ne rend pas moins réelles les réponses trouvées en chemin. Feynman disait qu’il pouvait vivre avec le doute et l’ignorance, et que c’était plus intéressant que d’avoir des réponses peut-être fausses.

Et « de rien à rien » oublie le milieu. Le milieu, c’est tout : les étoiles, les trous noirs, et quelqu’un qui, un soir tranquille, essaie de comprendre un article trop difficile pour lui. S’il n’y a pas de fin ultime, alors poser des questions n’est pas un échec à arriver. C’est peut-être ce que fait l’univers quand il devient assez complexe pour se regarder lui-même.

J’ai commencé en croyant que l’univers devait être simple. Je le crois toujours. Mais simple ne veut peut-être pas dire achevé.

Sources

  • Miyashita, Sekino et Susskind, Holograms and Standard Models (2026)
  • Entropie de Bekenstein–Hawking, Wikipédia
  • Blau, Guendelman et Guth, « Dynamics of false-vacuum bubbles », Physical Review D 35, 1747 (1987)

item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, October 2026. The code for the figures is here: figs.py.

In short. Experts learn slowly, once, and then act fast on habit. Most AI automation today does the opposite: an agent reasons from scratch on every run, which compounds errors, costs time and forgets what it learned. Fast AI uses the large model before the loop, as a compiler: it builds a structured memory once, and fast, explainable models run the process. The agentic loop is kept for the exceptions, and what it learns there becomes the next habit.

TipKey takeaways
  • An agentic loop interprets the task on every run. Fast AI compiles it.
  • Use the large model to build the memory, a knowledge graph experts can inspect and correct, not to replace it.
  • Let deep learning perceive and trees decide.
  • Keep the loop for the exceptions, and feed what it learns back into the memory.
  • It is worth it only for work that repeats; for one-off problems, the agent is the right tool.

1. Learning is slow, habits are fast

Think of a new accountant in their first week. Every invoice is a small investigation. They read it line by line, check the contract, look up the supplier, ask a colleague which budget it belongs to. Ten years later, the same person glances at an invoice and knows. They have not become a faster thinker. They have turned years of slow learning into fast habits.

This is how expertise works, in people and in most living things. Learning is slow and deliberate, and it happens rarely. Acting is fast and nearly automatic, and it happens constantly. The slow part builds a structure; the fast part uses it. When something truly new appears, the expert slows down again, thinks, and if the lesson is worth keeping, it becomes a new habit.

I call this idea Fast AI. Not fast because the hardware is quick, but fast because the thinking has already been done.

2. The agent that reads the manual every morning

Now look at how we build automation with AI today.

The typical agent receives a task, reads the context, reasons about what to do, calls a tool, reads the result, reasons again, calls another tool, and continues until it believes the task is done. It is impressive to watch. It is also an employee who arrives every morning with no memory and reads the whole manual again before touching anything.

For automation processes, this has four costs.

  • Errors compound. If each step is right 95% of the time, a 20-step loop gets everything right only about 36% of the time (0.95 to the power 20). Agents add checks and retries to compensate, which adds more steps, more time and more cost.
  • It is slow. Each step is a call to a large model that takes seconds. A process that runs ten thousand times a day pays that price ten thousand times, for reasoning that was nearly identical yesterday.
  • It is not repeatable. Give the same input twice and the agent may take a different path. In regulated work, the question is not only “is the answer right?” but “would it give the same answer tomorrow, and can you show me why?”. A loop of free-text reasoning is hard to audit and harder to certify.
  • It does not accumulate. What the agent figured out on Monday is gone on Tuesday, unless someone builds a memory around it. The intelligence is spent, not invested.

None of this means agents are bad. It means they are the wrong default for work that repeats.

3. Compile, don’t interpret

Programmers know this distinction well. An interpreter reads and executes a program line by line, every time it runs. A compiler reads the program once, works hard to understand and optimise it, and produces something that runs fast and identically, again and again.

An agentic loop interprets the task on every run. Fast AI compiles it.

In this view, the language model’s best role in automation is not to sit inside the loop. It is to work before the loop, as the compiler. It does the slow, intelligent work once: reading, extracting, structuring, connecting. Then it steps aside, and something fast and simple runs the process.

4. The slow part: a structured memory

What does the language model compile the domain into? My answer is a knowledge graph: a structured memory of the things in a domain and how they relate.

Language models are very good at the slow work this requires. Give them contracts, policies, past cases, emails and the notes experts leave behind, and they can extract the entities and relations hidden in all that text. For supplier invoices, that means suppliers, contracts, cost centres, approvers, products and the links between them: this supplier’s invoices go to this budget, amounts above this limit need a second approval, this kind of line item was disputed three times last year.

Three things make the graph more valuable than a pile of documents or a long prompt.

  • It is explicit. Every fact is a node and a link that a person can inspect, correct or delete. Experts can validate it, and they should, because extraction makes mistakes.
  • It is stable. It does not change between runs unless someone changes it. The same question gets the same facts.
  • It accumulates. Every new case, correction and exception can be added. The intelligence is invested, not spent.

This is the slow learning of the expert, written down.

5. The fast part: trees and networks together

With the memory in place, the decision itself rarely needs a large language model. It needs the right fast model, and here Fast AI has a second meaning: it is a hybrid, not deep learning everywhere.

Deep learning is unmatched at perception: turning raw, messy inputs such as images, scanned documents, sound or free text into meaningful features. Decision trees, and especially gradient-boosted trees, are often better at deciding: taking a table of meaningful features and producing a choice. On structured, tabular data, which describes most business decisions, well-tuned tree ensembles still match or beat deep networks in careful public benchmarks, while being faster, needing less data and being far easier to explain.

So the natural split is:

  • Deep networks perceive. They read the scanned invoice, the photo or the text of a request, and turn it into features.
  • The knowledge graph remembers. It supplies what is known about those features: past cases, rules, constraints.
  • Trees decide. They combine both into a decision in milliseconds, and they can show which features drove it.

Each part does what it is best at. None of them needs to think from scratch on every case.

6. The loop moves to where it belongs

Fast AI does not remove deliberation. It moves it.

The fast path handles the common cases. But every fast model should know when it is unsure: a low confidence score, a case unlike anything in its memory, a combination the graph has never seen. Those cases, and only those, go to the slow path: a language model reasoning through the problem, an agent exploring options, or a person.

And when the slow path solves a new case, the answer does not vanish. It goes back into the knowledge graph, and if it repeats, the fast models are retrained on it. Deliberation becomes habit. This is the expert again, slowing down only for the truly new, and learning from it.

So the agentic loop does not disappear. It stops running on every case and starts running on the exceptions, where its intelligence pays off.

7. An example: routing supplier invoices

Take a common task in any finance department: deciding what to do with each incoming invoice. Approve it, send it to the right person, or flag it.

The agentic way. An agent receives the invoice, calls a tool to read it, reasons about the supplier, searches the contracts, reasons about the amount, looks up the approval rules, proposes a route, checks it and adjusts. It may take half a minute, cost a noticeable amount, and route slightly differently next time. Explaining why it chose this approver means reading pages of its reasoning.

The Fast AI way. Months earlier, a language model read the contracts, policies and past decisions, and built a graph of suppliers, budgets, limits and approvers. The finance team reviewed it. Now, for each new invoice, a network reads the document, the graph supplies the relevant contract and history, and a tree ensemble picks a route in milliseconds. It explains its choice: supplier, amount against contract, cost centre, past disputes. When an invoice is unlike anything seen before, it says so and hands it to a person or an agent. Their answer enriches the graph.

Both use AI. Only one of them gets faster and better every month.

8. What Fast AI costs

This approach has real costs, and they are worth stating.

  • The graph is work. Extraction errors must be caught, and someone has to own the memory. A wrong fact in the graph is repeated quickly and confidently, which is worse than a slow mistake.
  • It needs repetition. For tasks that are truly one-off or open-ended, compiling makes no sense. There is nothing to reuse, and the agent is the right tool.
  • The world drifts. New suppliers, new rules, new products: a fast system can go on confidently applying old habits. It needs a monitor that notices when its decisions stop fitting, as my last essay argued for dashboards.
  • It takes design. An agent can be set up in an afternoon. A hybrid of graph, networks and trees takes engineering. That upfront cost is precisely the slow learning, and it pays off only if the process repeats enough.

9. Conclusion

We are tempted to put the most powerful model in the middle of every process, thinking on every run. For open problems, that is right. For automation, it is often like asking a senior expert to reread the whole manual before every routine job.

The alternative is older than AI. Learn slowly, once, and write down what you learned. Act fast, with simple tools you can explain. Slow down only when something is truly new, and turn what you learn there into the next habit.

Use the large model to build the memory, not to replace it. Let deep learning perceive and trees decide. Keep the loop for the exceptions. That is Fast AI: not less intelligence, but intelligence spent once and invested, instead of spent again on every run.

The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

item.description:
Essai, octobre 2026. Le code des figures est ici : figs.py. Les figures sont en anglais. Traduit de l’anglais : version originale.

En bref. Les experts apprennent lentement, une fois, puis agissent vite, par habitude. La plupart des automatisations par IA font aujourd’hui l’inverse : un agent raisonne à partir de zéro à chaque exécution, ce qui accumule les erreurs, coûte du temps et oublie ce qu’il a appris. Fast AI utilise le grand modèle avant la boucle, comme un compilateur : il construit une fois une mémoire structurée, puis des modèles rapides et explicables font tourner le processus. La boucle agentique est gardée pour les exceptions, et ce qu’elle y apprend devient la prochaine habitude.

AstuceÀ retenir
  • Une boucle agentique interprète la tâche à chaque exécution. Fast AI la compile.
  • Utiliser le grand modèle pour construire la mémoire, un graphe de connaissances que les experts peuvent inspecter et corriger, pas pour la remplacer.
  • Laisser l’apprentissage profond percevoir et les arbres décider.
  • Garder la boucle pour les exceptions, et réinjecter ce qu’elle apprend dans la mémoire.
  • Cela ne vaut la peine que pour un travail qui se répète ; pour les problèmes ponctuels, l’agent est le bon outil.

1. Apprendre est lent, les habitudes sont rapides

Pensez à un comptable débutant pendant sa première semaine. Chaque facture est une petite enquête. Il la lit ligne par ligne, vérifie le contrat, cherche le fournisseur, demande à un collègue à quel budget elle appartient. Dix ans plus tard, la même personne jette un coup d’œil à une facture et sait. Elle n’est pas devenue un penseur plus rapide. Elle a transformé des années d’apprentissage lent en habitudes rapides.

C’est ainsi que fonctionne l’expertise, chez les humains et chez la plupart des êtres vivants. Apprendre est lent et délibéré, et cela arrive rarement. Agir est rapide et presque automatique, et cela arrive en permanence. La partie lente construit une structure ; la partie rapide l’utilise. Quand quelque chose de vraiment nouveau apparaît, l’expert ralentit à nouveau, réfléchit, et si la leçon vaut la peine d’être gardée, elle devient une nouvelle habitude.

J’appelle cette idée Fast AI. Non pas rapide parce que le matériel est rapide, mais rapide parce que la réflexion a déjà été faite.

2. L’agent qui relit le manuel chaque matin

Regardons maintenant comment nous construisons aujourd’hui l’automatisation avec l’IA.

L’agent typique reçoit une tâche, lit le contexte, réfléchit à ce qu’il faut faire, appelle un outil, lit le résultat, réfléchit encore, appelle un autre outil, et continue jusqu’à ce qu’il estime la tâche terminée. C’est impressionnant à regarder. C’est aussi un employé qui arrive chaque matin sans mémoire et relit tout le manuel avant de toucher à quoi que ce soit.

Pour les processus d’automatisation, cela a quatre coûts.

  • Les erreurs s’accumulent. Si chaque étape est juste 95 % du temps, une boucle de 20 étapes n’est entièrement juste qu’environ 36 % du temps (0,95 à la puissance 20). Les agents ajoutent des vérifications et des nouvelles tentatives pour compenser, ce qui ajoute des étapes, du temps et des coûts.
  • C’est lent. Chaque étape est un appel à un grand modèle qui prend des secondes. Un processus qui tourne dix mille fois par jour paie ce prix dix mille fois, pour un raisonnement presque identique à celui de la veille.
  • Ce n’est pas reproductible. Donnez deux fois la même entrée, et l’agent peut prendre un chemin différent. Dans un travail réglementé, la question n’est pas seulement « la réponse est-elle juste ? », mais « donnerait-il la même réponse demain, et pouvez-vous me montrer pourquoi ? ». Une boucle de raisonnement en texte libre est difficile à auditer et plus difficile encore à certifier.
  • Rien ne s’accumule. Ce que l’agent a compris lundi a disparu mardi, à moins que quelqu’un ne construise une mémoire autour. L’intelligence est dépensée, pas investie.

Rien de tout cela ne veut dire que les agents sont mauvais. Cela veut dire qu’ils sont le mauvais choix par défaut pour un travail qui se répète.

3. Compiler, pas interpréter

Les programmeurs connaissent bien cette distinction. Un interpréteur lit et exécute un programme ligne par ligne, à chaque exécution. Un compilateur lit le programme une fois, travaille dur pour le comprendre et l’optimiser, et produit quelque chose qui tourne vite et de façon identique, encore et encore.

Une boucle agentique interprète la tâche à chaque exécution. Fast AI la compile.

Dans cette vision, le meilleur rôle du modèle de langage dans l’automatisation n’est pas d’être dans la boucle. Il est de travailler avant la boucle, comme compilateur. Il fait une fois le travail lent et intelligent : lire, extraire, structurer, relier. Puis il s’efface, et quelque chose de rapide et simple fait tourner le processus.

4. La partie lente : une mémoire structurée

En quoi le modèle de langage compile-t-il le domaine ? Ma réponse est un graphe de connaissances : une mémoire structurée des choses d’un domaine et de leurs relations.

Les modèles de langage sont très bons pour le travail lent que cela demande. Donnez-leur des contrats, des règlements, des cas passés, des e-mails et les notes que laissent les experts, et ils peuvent extraire les entités et les relations cachées dans tout ce texte. Pour les factures fournisseurs, cela veut dire les fournisseurs, les contrats, les centres de coûts, les approbateurs, les produits et les liens entre eux : les factures de ce fournisseur vont sur ce budget, les montants au-dessus de cette limite demandent une seconde approbation, ce type de ligne a été contesté trois fois l’an dernier.

Trois choses rendent le graphe plus précieux qu’une pile de documents ou qu’un long prompt.

  • Il est explicite. Chaque fait est un nœud et un lien qu’une personne peut inspecter, corriger ou supprimer. Les experts peuvent le valider, et ils devraient le faire, car l’extraction fait des erreurs.
  • Il est stable. Il ne change pas d’une exécution à l’autre, sauf si quelqu’un le modifie. La même question obtient les mêmes faits.
  • Il s’accumule. Chaque nouveau cas, chaque correction et chaque exception peuvent y être ajoutés. L’intelligence est investie, pas dépensée.

C’est l’apprentissage lent de l’expert, mis par écrit.

5. La partie rapide : arbres et réseaux ensemble

Une fois la mémoire en place, la décision elle-même a rarement besoin d’un grand modèle de langage. Elle a besoin du bon modèle rapide, et Fast AI prend ici un second sens : c’est un hybride, pas de l’apprentissage profond partout.

L’apprentissage profond est inégalé pour la perception : transformer des entrées brutes et désordonnées, comme des images, des documents scannés, du son ou du texte libre, en caractéristiques qui ont du sens. Les arbres de décision, et surtout les arbres boostés par gradient, sont souvent meilleurs pour décider : prendre un tableau de caractéristiques et produire un choix. Sur des données structurées en tableaux, qui décrivent la plupart des décisions d’entreprise, des ensembles d’arbres bien réglés égalent ou battent encore les réseaux profonds dans des comparaisons publiques soignées, tout en étant plus rapides, en demandant moins de données et en étant bien plus faciles à expliquer.

Le partage naturel est donc :

  • Les réseaux profonds perçoivent. Ils lisent la facture scannée, la photo ou le texte d’une demande, et les transforment en caractéristiques.
  • Le graphe de connaissances se souvient. Il fournit ce que l’on sait de ces caractéristiques : cas passés, règles, contraintes.
  • Les arbres décident. Ils combinent les deux en une décision en quelques millisecondes, et peuvent montrer quelles caractéristiques l’ont déterminée.

Chaque partie fait ce qu’elle fait le mieux. Aucune n’a besoin de réfléchir à partir de zéro pour chaque cas.

6. La boucle va là où elle a sa place

Fast AI ne supprime pas la délibération. Il la déplace.

Le chemin rapide traite les cas courants. Mais chaque modèle rapide devrait savoir quand il n’est pas sûr : un score de confiance faible, un cas qui ne ressemble à rien dans sa mémoire, une combinaison que le graphe n’a jamais vue. Ces cas, et seulement ceux-là, partent vers le chemin lent : un modèle de langage qui raisonne sur le problème, un agent qui explore les options, ou une personne.

Et quand le chemin lent résout un nouveau cas, la réponse ne disparaît pas. Elle retourne dans le graphe de connaissances, et si elle se répète, les modèles rapides sont réentraînés avec elle. La délibération devient habitude. C’est à nouveau l’expert, qui ne ralentit que pour le vraiment nouveau, et qui en tire une leçon.

La boucle agentique ne disparaît donc pas. Elle cesse de tourner sur chaque cas et se met à tourner sur les exceptions, là où son intelligence rapporte.

7. Un exemple : l’acheminement des factures fournisseurs

Prenons une tâche courante dans tout service financier : décider quoi faire de chaque facture qui arrive. L’approuver, l’envoyer à la bonne personne, ou la signaler.

La manière agentique. Un agent reçoit la facture, appelle un outil pour la lire, raisonne sur le fournisseur, cherche dans les contrats, raisonne sur le montant, consulte les règles d’approbation, propose un circuit, le vérifie et l’ajuste. Cela peut prendre une demi-minute, coûter une somme non négligeable, et donner un circuit légèrement différent la fois suivante. Expliquer pourquoi il a choisi cet approbateur demande de lire des pages de son raisonnement.

La manière Fast AI. Des mois plus tôt, un modèle de langage a lu les contrats, les règlements et les décisions passées, et a construit un graphe des fournisseurs, des budgets, des limites et des approbateurs. L’équipe financière l’a relu. Maintenant, pour chaque nouvelle facture, un réseau lit le document, le graphe fournit le contrat et l’historique pertinents, et un ensemble d’arbres choisit un circuit en quelques millisecondes. Il explique son choix : fournisseur, montant par rapport au contrat, centre de coûts, litiges passés. Quand une facture ne ressemble à rien de connu, il le dit et la passe à une personne ou à un agent. Leur réponse enrichit le graphe.

Les deux utilisent l’IA. Une seule devient plus rapide et meilleure chaque mois.

8. Ce que coûte Fast AI

Cette approche a de vrais coûts, et il vaut la peine de les dire.

  • Le graphe demande du travail. Il faut repérer les erreurs d’extraction, et quelqu’un doit être responsable de la mémoire. Un fait faux dans le graphe est répété vite et avec assurance, ce qui est pire qu’une erreur lente.
  • Il faut de la répétition. Pour des tâches vraiment ponctuelles ou ouvertes, compiler n’a pas de sens. Il n’y a rien à réutiliser, et l’agent est le bon outil.
  • Le monde dérive. Nouveaux fournisseurs, nouvelles règles, nouveaux produits : un système rapide peut continuer à appliquer avec assurance de vieilles habitudes. Il lui faut un moniteur qui remarque quand ses décisions ne collent plus, comme mon dernier essai (en anglais) le défendait pour les tableaux de bord.
  • Il faut de la conception. Un agent se met en place en un après-midi. Un hybride de graphe, de réseaux et d’arbres demande de l’ingénierie. Ce coût initial est précisément l’apprentissage lent, et il n’est rentable que si le processus se répète assez.

9. Conclusion

Nous sommes tentés de placer le modèle le plus puissant au milieu de chaque processus, à réfléchir à chaque exécution. Pour les problèmes ouverts, c’est juste. Pour l’automatisation, c’est souvent comme demander à un expert chevronné de relire tout le manuel avant chaque tâche de routine.

L’alternative est plus ancienne que l’IA. Apprendre lentement, une fois, et mettre par écrit ce que l’on a appris. Agir vite, avec des outils simples que l’on peut expliquer. Ne ralentir que quand quelque chose est vraiment nouveau, et transformer ce que l’on y apprend en prochaine habitude.

Utiliser le grand modèle pour construire la mémoire, pas pour la remplacer. Laisser l’apprentissage profond percevoir et les arbres décider. Garder la boucle pour les exceptions. C’est cela, Fast AI : pas moins d’intelligence, mais une intelligence dépensée une fois et investie, au lieu d’être dépensée à nouveau à chaque exécution.

Les opinions exprimées dans cet essai sont les miennes et ne décrivent aucun produit ni aucun projet de mon employeur.
